## Appendix A Reparametrization mode three-point interaction on the circle

In this section, we rederive the result for the three-point interaction of the reparametrization modes given in (4.14), working with the reparametrization action on the circle rather than on the line. Doing the analysis on the circle allows us to handle the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ zero modes more explicitly.

We will focus only on the contribution of the interacting diagrams on the circle, and will not rederive the full connected six-point function. Recall that we write the boundary mode on the circle as $\tilde{\alpha}(\tau)=\tau+\tilde{\epsilon}(\tau)$ , where $\tilde{\epsilon}$ is a small perturbation around the saddle point that we can expand in Fourier modes: $\epsilon(\tau)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}e^{-in\tau}$ . Here, $n=0,\pm 1$ are zero modes of the action that need to be gauge fixed in the reparametrization path integral.

The two ingredients we need to study the three-point reparametrization interaction diagrams are the reparametrization action to cubic order in $\tilde{\epsilon}$ and the dressed two-point function to linear order. After adding a gauge-fixing term $S_{\rm gf}$ , the full action to cubic order is:

$$ \displaystyle S_{L} \displaystyle=S_{\rm gf}+S_{L,2}+S_{L,3}+O(\tilde{\epsilon}^{4}), $$

where $S_{L,2}$ and $S_{L,3}$ are given in (3.39) and we pick the gauge-fixing term to be:

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm gf} \displaystyle=T_{s}\left[\frac{1}{2a}\tilde{\epsilon}_{0}^{2}+\frac{1}{b}\tilde{\epsilon}_{1}\tilde{\epsilon}_{-1}\right]. $$

From the combined quadratic piece $S_{\rm gf}+S_{L,2}$ , we read off the Wick contraction of the Fourier modes:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{m}\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}\rangle_{0} \displaystyle=f_{m}\delta_{m+n,0}, \displaystyle f_{m} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{T_{s}}\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}a&m=0\\
b&m=\pm 1\\
\frac{1}{4\pi}\frac{1}{|n|(n^{2}-1)}&\text{otherwise}\end{array}\right. $$

A simple gauge choice is to set $a=b=0$ , which amounts to excluding the $n=0,\pm 1$ modes from $\tilde{\epsilon}(\tau)$ , but we can keep $a$ and $b$ general. The $\epsilon$ position space propagator is then:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\epsilon(\tau_{1})\epsilon(\tau_{2})\rangle_{0} \displaystyle=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{n}e^{-in\tau_{12}}=\frac{1}{T_{s}}\left[a+2b\cos{\tau_{12}}+\frac{1}{4\pi}\sum_{n\neq 0,\pm 1}\frac{e^{-in\tau_{12}}}{|n|(n^{2}-1)}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{T_{s}}\left[a-\frac{1}{4\pi}+\left(2b+\frac{3}{8\pi}\right)\cos(\tau_{12})+\frac{1}{2\pi}\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\tau_{12}}{2}\right)\log\left(4\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\tau_{12}}{2}\right)\right)\right]. $$

Note that (up to a relabelling of $a$ and $b$ ), this is related to (4.4) by the usual interchange of euclidean distances on the line and chordal distances on the circle.

Meanwhile, the dressed-two point function on the circle $B^{\rm circle}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})$ is given in (2.35), where $\tilde{\beta}$ is the inverse of $\tilde{\alpha}$ , which to linear order in $\tilde{\epsilon}$ is $\tilde{\beta}(\theta)=\theta-\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta)+O(\tilde{\epsilon}^{2})$ . The expansion of the normalized dressed two-point function is then:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) \displaystyle\equiv\bigg[2\sin{\frac{\theta_{12}}{2}}\bigg]^{2}B^{\rm circle}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})=1+\mathcal{B}_{1}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})+O(\tilde{\epsilon}^{2}), $$

where the linear piece is explicitly

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{1}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2}) \displaystyle=-\dot{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{1}-\dot{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{2}+\cot{\frac{\theta_{12}}{2}}\tilde{\epsilon}_{12}, $$

where we use the shorthand $\dot{\tilde{\epsilon}}_{n}=\dot{\tilde{\epsilon}}(\theta_{n})$ and $\tilde{\epsilon}_{ij}=\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{i})-\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{j})$ . Knowing $\mathcal{B}_{1}$ is sufficient to study the contribution of the three-point diagrams to the connected six-point function, which in analogy with (4.10) is given by:

$$ \displaystyle-\langle\mathcal{B}_{1}(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})\mathcal{B}_{1}(\theta_{3},\theta_{4})\mathcal{B}_{1}(\theta_{5},\theta_{6})S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,c}, $$

Here “c” stands for “connected” and tells us to contract the $\tilde{\epsilon}$ ’s in the $\mathcal{B}_{1}$ ’s with the three $\tilde{\epsilon}$ ’s in the cubic action. To compute the full connected six-point function, we would also need the quadratic piece $\mathcal{B}_{2}$ .

We will now compute the three-point interacting diagram:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{1})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,\text{c}}=\sum_{a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-ia\theta_{1}-ib\theta_{2}-ic\theta_{3}}\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{a}\tilde{\epsilon}_{b}\tilde{\epsilon}_{c}S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,\text{c}} $$

Given the expression for the cubic action in (3.39) and using the propagator in (A) to Wick contract the different Fourier modes, we have

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{a}\tilde{\epsilon}_{b}\tilde{\epsilon}_{c}S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,\text{c}} \displaystyle=-2i\pi T_{s}\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\text{sgn}(p)p^{2}(p^{2}-1)\big[\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{a}\tilde{\epsilon}_{m}\rangle_{0}\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{b}\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}\rangle_{0}\langle\tilde{\epsilon}_{c}\tilde{\epsilon}_{p}\rangle_{0}+a\leftrightarrow c+b\leftrightarrow c\big] \displaystyle=-2i\pi T_{s}\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\text{sgn}(p)p^{2}(p^{2}-1)\big[f_{m}f_{n}f_{p}\delta_{m+a,0}\delta_{n+b,0}\delta_{p+c,0}+a\leftrightarrow c+b\leftrightarrow c\big] $$

(Recall that $p=-m-n$ ). Substituting this into (A.11) and using the three Kronecker deltas to fix $a$ , $b$ and $c$ , we find:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{1})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,\text{c}} \displaystyle=-2i\pi T_{s}\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}\text{sgn}(p)p^{2}(p^{2}-1)f_{m}f_{n}f_{p}\left[e^{im\theta_{13}+in\theta_{23}}+\theta_{1}\leftrightarrow\theta_{2}+\theta_{2}\leftrightarrow\theta_{3}\right] \displaystyle=-\frac{i}{2}\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{n}p(1-\delta_{p,1}-\delta_{p,-1})\left[e^{im\theta_{13}+in\theta_{23}}+\theta_{1}\leftrightarrow\theta_{3}+\theta_{2}\leftrightarrow\theta_{3}\right]. $$

To get to the second line, we used $f_{p}\text{sgn}(p)p^{2}=\frac{p}{4\pi T_{s}}(1-\delta_{p,1}-\delta_{p,-1})$ , which follows from (A). Let’s focus on one term inside the square bracket in (A.13) at a time. There are three different contributions to the sum over $m$ and $n$ , corresponding to the “1,” the “ $-\delta_{p,1}$ ” and the “ $-\delta_{p,-1}$ ” in $1-\delta_{p,1}-\delta_{p,-1}$ . The first is the simplest:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{i}{2}\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{n}(m+n)e^{-im\theta_{13}-in\theta_{23}} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{3}\biggr[\sum_{m}f_{m}e^{im\theta_{13}}\sum_{n}f_{n}e^{in\theta_{23}}\biggr], \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{3}[\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{1})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})\rangle_{0}\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})\rangle_{0}]. $$

To get to the second line we used (A.6). In direct analogy with (4.14), we see that the double sum breaks into a product of single sums. This implies that the three-point interaction diagram effectively “factorizes” in terms of products of the $\epsilon$ propagator, as long as the contributions from the “ $-\delta_{p,1}$ ” and the “ $-\delta_{p,-1}$ ” to (A.13) can be neglected. We now show that is indeed the case.

We need to compute:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{n}p\delta_{p,1}e^{im\theta_{13}+in\theta_{23}}=e^{-i\theta_{23}}\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{-m-1}e^{im\theta_{12}} \displaystyle\sum_{m,n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{n}p\delta_{p,-1}e^{im\theta_{13}+in\theta_{23}}=-e^{i\theta_{23}}\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}f_{m}f_{-m+1}e^{im\theta_{12}} $$

Given that $f_{m}=f_{-m}$ , (A.16) is minus the complex conjugate of (A.15). The last piece that we need to evaluate is then:

$$ \displaystyle k(\theta)\equiv\sum_{m}f_{m}f_{-m-1}e^{im\theta}=\frac{ab}{T_{s}^{2}}\left(1+e^{-i\theta}\right) \displaystyle+\frac{b}{24\pi T_{s}^{2}}(e^{i\theta}+e^{-2i\theta}) \displaystyle+\frac{1}{16\pi^{2}T_{s}^{2}}\sum_{m\neq-2,-1,0,1}\frac{e^{im\theta}}{|m||m+1|m(m^{2}-1)(m+2)}. $$

The remaining sum in (A.17) can be evaluated and simplifies to:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{m\neq-2,-1,0,1}\frac{e^{im\theta}}{|m||m+1|m(m^{2}-1)(m+2)}=\frac{e^{-\frac{i\theta}{2}}}{36}\biggr( \displaystyle 3(33-4\pi^{2}+12\pi|\theta|-6\theta^{2})\cos{\frac{\theta}{2}}+20\cos{\frac{3\theta}{2}} \displaystyle+6(|\theta|-\pi)(9\sin{\frac{|\theta|}{2}}+\sin{\frac{3|\theta|}{2}})\biggr). $$

Combining (A.14)-(A.17), eq. (A.13) becomes

$$ \displaystyle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{1})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})S_{L,3}\rangle_{0,\text{c}} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\theta_{1}}\left[\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{1})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\rangle\langle\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{2})\tilde{\epsilon}(\theta_{3})\rangle\right]+1\leftrightarrow 2+1\leftrightarrow 3+R(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3}) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle R(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3}) \displaystyle=\frac{i}{2}\left(e^{-i\theta_{23}}k(\theta_{12})-e^{i\theta_{23}}k(\theta_{12})^{*}\right)+1\leftrightarrow 2+1\leftrightarrow 3. $$

Eq. (A.19) almost matches eq. (4.14), which we derived working on the line and using analytic regularization to handle the zero modes, except that (A.19) has the extra term $R(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3})$ . This term is not zero, but we claim that it does not contribute to (A.10), and therefore can be neglected in the computation of the connected six-point function on the circle. Concretely, the claim is that if we expand each $\mathcal{B}_{1}$ in (A.10) into four $\tilde{\epsilon}$ terms according to (A.9), apply (A.19) to the $64$ different terms, and then sum up all the terms, the contribution from $R$ is zero. This appears tedious to check analytically, but we confirmed it numerically within machine precision for a random sample of values for $\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{6}$ .

The rest of the computation of the connected six-point function on the circle proceeds in direct analogy with the computation on the line presented in section 4. The final result— after mapping chordal distances to euclidean distances— matches (4.33).

## Appendix B A conformal bilocal reparametrization action

In this appendix, we give a closed form expression for a bilocal reparametrization action that has the same symmetries as the AdS2 string reparametrization action defined in (2.14). Curiously, the action also precisely matches the string reparametrization action at quadratic and cubic order in the saddle point expansion (but apparently not at higher orders; see footnote 4).

Consider the following bilocal reparametrization action:

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm bilocal}[\alpha] \displaystyle=-C\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt_{1}dt_{2}\left[\left[\frac{\dot{\alpha}(t_{1})\dot{\alpha}(t_{2})}{(\alpha(t_{1})-\alpha(t_{2}))^{2}}\right]^{h}\frac{1}{|t_{12}|^{2-2h+\eta}}-\frac{1}{|t_{12}|^{2+\eta}}\right]. $$

Here, $\alpha(t)$ is a reparametrization of the line, $h$ and $\eta$ are real parameters, and $C$ is a coupling constant with mass dimension $[C]=\eta$ . This action was studied for the case $2-2h+\eta=0$ in [70, 71], and discussed for the case $\eta=0$ towards the end of appendix G of [33]. We have added a $-1/|t_{12}|^{2+\eta}$ counterterm to make the action finite in the coincident limit $t_{2}\to t_{1}$ as long as $\eta<1$ ;1818 18 The finiteness of (B.1) follows from the fact that in the coincident limit $\displaystyle\frac{\dot{\alpha}(t_{1})\dot{\alpha}(t_{2})}{(\alpha(t_{1})-\alpha(t_{2}))^{2}}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{t_{12}^{2}}+\frac{1}{6}\{\alpha,t_{1}\}+O(t_{1}-t_{2}),$ $\displaystyle t_{2}\to t_{1},$ (B.2) where $\{\alpha,t\}=-\frac{3}{2}\frac{\ddot{\alpha}^{2}}{\dot{\alpha}^{2}}+\frac{\dddot{\alpha}}{\dot{\alpha}}$ is the Schwarzian derivative. the counterterm is zero in analytic regularization.

We are interested in (B.1) when $\eta\to 0$ . In this special case, the action has two $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ symmetries, just like the string reparametrization action in (2.14), and it is therefore “conformal.” To see this, let $f(t)=\frac{at+b}{ct+d}$ denote a general $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ transformation and let $\alpha_{r}(t)=\alpha(f(t))$ and $\alpha_{\ell}(t)=f(\alpha(t))$ . Given that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{\ell}(t_{1})\dot{\alpha}_{\ell}(t_{2})}{(\alpha_{\ell}(t_{1})-\alpha_{\ell}(t_{2}))^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{\dot{\alpha}(t_{1})\dot{\alpha}(t_{2})}{(\alpha(t_{1})\alpha(t_{2}))^{2}}, \displaystyle\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{r}(t_{1})\dot{\alpha}_{r}(t_{2})}{(\alpha_{r}(t_{1})-\alpha_{r}(t_{2}))^{2}} \displaystyle=\dot{f}(t_{1})\dot{f}(t_{2})\frac{\dot{\alpha}(f(t_{1}))\dot{\alpha}(f(t_{2}))}{(\alpha(f(t_{1}))-\alpha(f(t_{2})))^{2}}, \displaystyle\frac{\dot{f}(t_{1})\dot{f}(t_{2})}{(f(t_{1})-f(t_{2}))^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{t_{12}^{2}}, $$

one can readily check that $S_{\rm bilocal}$ is invariant under $\alpha\to\alpha_{\ell}$ for any $\eta$ and invariant under $\alpha\to\alpha_{r}$ when $\eta\to 0$ .

Now consider the expansion of the action in (B.1) about the saddle point by letting $\alpha(t)=t+\epsilon(t)$ and expanding in $\epsilon$ . Using (C.1) and integration by parts to simplify the result, we find

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm bilocal} \displaystyle=2Ch(1-h)\bigg[\int dt_{1}dt_{2}\frac{\epsilon(t_{1})\epsilon(t_{2})}{|t_{12}|^{4+\eta}}-2\int dt_{1}dt_{2}\frac{\epsilon(t_{1})^{2}\epsilon(t_{2})}{|t_{12}|^{4+\eta}t_{12}} \displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{2}\int dt_{1}dt_{2}\biggr((1+2h)(3-2h)\frac{\frac{4}{3}\epsilon(t_{1})^{3}\epsilon(t_{2})-\epsilon(t_{1})^{2}\epsilon(t_{2})^{2}}{|t_{12}|^{6+\eta}} \displaystyle\quad+h(1-h)\frac{-2\epsilon(t_{1})\dot{\epsilon}(t_{1})^{2}\epsilon(t_{2})+\dot{\epsilon}(t_{1})^{2}\epsilon(t_{2})^{2}-\frac{1}{4}t_{12}^{2}\dot{\epsilon}(t_{1})^{2}\dot{\epsilon}(t_{2})^{2}}{|t_{12}|^{4+\eta}}\biggr)+O(\epsilon^{5})\biggr]. $$

To put this in the Fourier representation, we write $\epsilon(t)=\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}e^{-i\omega t}\epsilon(\omega)$ and evaluate the $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ integrals using (C.2)-(C.3). This leads to:

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm bilocal} \displaystyle=\frac{Ch(1-h)}{6}\biggr[\int d\omega\epsilon(\omega)\epsilon(-\omega)|\omega|^{3}-\frac{i}{4\pi}\int d\omega_{1}d\omega_{2}\epsilon(\omega_{1})\epsilon(\omega_{2})\epsilon(-\omega_{1}-\omega_{2})|\omega_{2}|^{4}\text{sgn}(\omega_{2}) \displaystyle-\pi\left(\int\prod_{i=1}^{4}\frac{d\omega_{i}}{2\pi}\epsilon(\omega_{i})\right)2\pi\delta\big(\sum_{i=1}^{4}\omega_{i}\big)\biggr[\frac{(1+2h)(3-2h)}{20}\big(\frac{4|\omega_{4}|^{5}}{3}-|\omega_{3}+\omega_{4}|^{5}\big) \displaystyle+h(1-h)\bigg(-2|\omega_{4}|^{3}\omega_{1}\omega_{2}+|\omega_{3}+\omega_{4}|^{3}\omega_{1}\omega_{2}-\frac{3}{2}|\omega_{3}+\omega_{4}|\omega_{1}\omega_{2}\omega_{3}\omega_{4}\bigg)\biggr]+O(\epsilon^{5})\biggr] $$

As promised, the action in (B.6) precisely matches the string reparametrization action to cubic order given in (3.20) and (3.31), as long as we set $C=\frac{3T_{s}}{\pi h(1-h)}$ .

The analog of (B.1) on the circle (with the counterterm set to zero for simplicity) is:

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm bilocal}[\alpha] \displaystyle=-C\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\bigg[\frac{\dot{\alpha}(\tau_{1})\dot{\alpha}(\tau_{2})}{\big[2\sin{\frac{\alpha(\tau_{1})-\alpha(\tau_{2})}{2}}\big]^{2}}\bigg]^{h}\frac{1}{\left|2\sin{\frac{\tau_{12}}{2}}\right|^{2-2h+\eta}}. $$

If we set $\alpha(\tau)=\tau+\tilde{\epsilon}(\tau)$ , expand in $\tilde{\epsilon}$ , and use (C.4) and integration by parts to simplify terms, we again find that the bilocal action on the circle matches the string reparametrization action given in (3.34) to cubic order.

#### Conformal $k$ -local conformal reparametrization.

Note that (B.1) is constructed by multiplying a reparametrization-dressed conformal two-point function with an undressed two-point function. It is easy to generalize (B.1) and write down a $k$ -local action invariant under two $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ symmetries starting from a pair of conformal $k$ -point functions. In particular, let

$$ \displaystyle G(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k})=\langle O_{h_{1}}(t_{1})\ldots O_{h_{k}}(t_{k})\rangle, $$

be any correlator in a 1d CFT of $k$ operators $O_{h_{i}}$ with conformal dimensions $h_{i}$ , and let

$$ \displaystyle\bar{G}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k})=\langle\bar{O}_{1-h_{1}}(t_{1})\ldots\bar{O}_{1-h_{k}}(t_{k})\rangle, $$

be any correlator in a 1d CFT of $k$ operators $\bar{O}_{1-h_{i}}$ with conformal dimensions $1-h_{i}$ . Then we define the reparametrization action

$$ \displaystyle S_{k-\text{local}}[\alpha(t)] \displaystyle=C\int\prod_{i=1}^{k}dt_{i}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\dot{\alpha}(t_{i})^{h_{i}}G(\alpha(t_{1}),\ldots,\alpha(t_{n}))\bar{G}(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}). $$

This action is also invariant under both $\alpha(t)\to f(\alpha(t))$ and $\alpha(t)\to\alpha(f(t))$ , where $f$ is a general $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ transformation. This follows from (B.3)-(B.5) together with the conformal Ward identity, which says that

$$ \displaystyle G(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k}) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\dot{f}(t_{i})^{h_{i}}G(f(t_{1}),\ldots,f(t_{k})), $$

and with an analogous statement for $\bar{G}$ .

Within this construction, (B.11) is unique to the extent that the $k$ -pt function in 1d CFT is unique. For instance, the bilocal action is unique up to normalization $C$ and choice of conformal dimension $h$ , and the $3$ -local action is unique up to normalization and choice of three conformal dimensions $h_{1}$ , $h_{2}$ , $h_{3}$ .

## Appendix C Useful integrals for analytic regularization

In analytic regularization, the following identities hold on the line:

$$ \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\frac{1}{|t|^{\Delta}} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\frac{e^{i\omega t}}{|t|^{\Delta}} \displaystyle=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\Delta\right)\Gamma(1-\Delta)|\omega|^{\Delta-1}, \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\frac{e^{i\omega t}}{|t|^{\Delta}t} \displaystyle=-2i\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\Delta\right)\Gamma(-\Delta)\text{sgn}(\omega)|\omega|^{\Delta}. $$

(The third identity is essentially the derivative of the second identity with respect to $\omega$ ). Likewise, the following identities hold on the circle:

$$ \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}d\tau\frac{1}{|2\sin{\frac{\tau}{2}}|^{\Delta}} \displaystyle=2^{1-\Delta}\sqrt{\pi}\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{1-\Delta}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(1-\frac{\Delta}{2}\right)}, \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}d\tau\frac{e^{in\tau}}{|2\sin{\frac{\tau}{2}}|^{\Delta}} \displaystyle=\frac{2\pi(-1)^{n}\Gamma(1-\Delta)}{\Gamma(1-n-\frac{\Delta}{2})\Gamma(1+n-\frac{\Delta}{2})}, \displaystyle\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}. $$
